prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All right, I admit it: It was just a dream I had last night. I was trudging along a muddy path in a column of downcast men on the blackened outskirts of New York, the twilight dingy and ruined, the future without hope as we marched along in our soiled, proletarian rags. To my left was Mayakovsky, head shaved, and next to him his friend with gray beard and dark cap. "You've got to admit," Mayakovsky was saying, "that this is a pretty good way to write a poem." "Yes," I said, "the momentum is sustained by our walking forward, the desolate landscape seeps into every word, and you're free to say anything you want." "That's because we're inside the poem," he said, "not outside." Puddles of oily water gleamed dully beneath the low clouds. "That's why my poems were so big: there's more room inside." The hard line of his jaw flexed and the men dispersed. I followed his friend behind a wall to hear the poem go on in the lecture the friend was giving on history, but no, the real poem had finished. I went back to the spot where the poem had finished. Vladimir had left the poem.

outputs.L3:
# The Dream

I dreamed I was walking through the bleak outskirts of New York, some blasted industrial edge of the city where the war had left its residue in twisted metal and broken concrete, everything cast in the grey-violet light of a twilight that seemed to have no beginning and no end. Around me marched a column of men, their heads bowed, their shoulders slumped beneath the weight of some invisible burden, all of us moving forward through this desolate landscape toward a destination none of us could name. The sky pressed down close and colorless, and the ground beneath our feet was littered with the debris of some catastrophe I could not quite remember or understand.

Mayakovsky walked beside me. His head was shaved, gleaming faintly in that strange dream-light, and his stride was purposeful even amid the general despondency of the march. He turned to me and said, with the particular certainty he always carried in his voice, that this—this exact scenario, this bleak marching through ruin—was precisely the way to compose a poem.

I found myself agreeing immediately, as one does in dreams, understanding suddenly and completely what he meant. There was something in the forward momentum of walking, in the rhythm of feet against broken pavement, in the desolation stretching out on every side, that infused the words with meaning before they were even spoken. The bleakness was not an obstacle to poetry but its very condition—it stripped away pretense, left only the essential motion of body and language moving together toward the same unknown point. Within that stark landscape I felt an unaccountable freedom, as though the emptiness of the surroundings had emptied out all the usual constraints, leaving room for whatever might need to be said.

Mayakovsky continued speaking as we walked, explaining that the power he and I possessed as poets came not from standing outside the poem, observing it, shaping it from some external vantage point of control, but from being inside it—submerged in its motion, subject to its logic, carried along by it as we were being carried now through this ruined landscape. This, he said, was why his own poems had always felt so expansive, so capable of containing multitudes: he had never stood apart from them. He had always been marching within.

I understood this too, in the way one understands things in dreams, with a clarity that does not require explanation. And then, as dreams do, it shifted. I was searching for the continuation of the poem—the poem that Mayakovsky and I had been composing simply by walking—and my search led me to a lecture being given by a friend of his, someone who might know how the poem went on, where it led, what came next in that long march through the twilight ruins.

But when I arrived, I understood that I was already too late. The poem had ended. It had ended somewhere back in that landscape, in some line I had not marked as the last line, in some step I had not recognized as the final step. And Vladimir was gone.
outputs.L4:
I dreamed I was walking through New York, though it was not the New York I knew. The city had been stripped of its usual clamor—no yellow cabs, no crowds spilling from subway grates, no neon bleeding into the night sky. Instead, the streets stretched out gray and silent, the buildings hollowed as if evacuated decades ago, their windows dark sockets staring down at empty avenues. Ash, or something like ash, drifted in the air, settling on abandoned cars and cracked pavement. It felt like the aftermath of something—a war, a plague, an ending whose details had been erased, leaving only the bare fact of desolation.

I was not alone. Beside me walked Mayakovsky, unmistakable in his broad-shouldered coat, his face set in that severe, declarative expression I recognized from old photographs. He did not seem surprised by the ruined city, nor by my presence at his side. We walked together as though continuing a conversation that had begun long before I arrived in the dream, our footsteps the only sound in that vast quiet.

He was speaking about poems—about the difference between writing from outside a poem and writing from within it. "When you stand outside," he said, his voice carrying that clipped, insistent rhythm I associated with his verse, "you see the poem as a shape, a thing to be measured and judged. You circle it. You describe it. But when you are inside—ah, inside there are no walls. Inside, the poem is the world, and you can move in every direction at once." He gestured at the ruined buildings around us, as if the city itself were an illustration of his point—a vast, broken structure that could only be understood by walking through its collapsed rooms rather than observing it from a distance.

I asked him what he meant, though some part of me already understood, the way one understands things in dreams—not through logic but through a kind of immediate, wordless recognition. He said that the poets who stayed outside their poems were always constrained by the shape they imagined, boxed in by expectation, while those who entered fully could stretch the poem's boundaries outward, discovering rooms that hadn't existed before they stepped inside. Freedom, he insisted, was not the absence of structure but the willingness to inhabit it completely, to let the structure become permeable from within.

We continued walking as he spoke, passing through what might have once been Times Square, its towering screens now blank and dead, hanging like dark mirrors reflecting nothing. The devastation around us seemed to swell with each block, and yet the conversation continued undisturbed, as though the ideas he offered were somehow more solid, more real, than the crumbling city itself.

Then, without any warning, the ground beneath the words began to give way. Mayakovsky's sentences grew fainter, their edges blurring like ink bleeding into water. I tried to hold onto what he had been saying, tried to keep pace with him, but the city around us was dissolving too—the buildings thinning into mist, the streets losing their solidity, becoming suggestion rather than substance. I turned to ask him something, some final question meant to anchor the moment, but he was already turning away, his form receding into the gray as though he had never fully belonged to that landscape in the first place.

I called after him, but no sound came. The poem we had been walking through—the desolate city, the philosophy of interiority, the very presence of the poet himself—was slipping away with the same suddenness with which it had arrived. I woke with the distinct sensation of having grasped something profound only to watch it evaporate before I could write it down, the way inspiration so often visits and departs, leaving behind only the faint impression that something had been there, something urgent and alive, now gone.
outputs.L5:
# The New York That Never Was

All cities carry ghosts, but New York carries more than most—entire versions of itself layered beneath the one you're walking through. Every corner holds the memory of what stood there before, and the promise of what will replace it next.

Consider the phrase itself: *All New York*. It suggests a totality that the city never actually delivers. No one experiences all of New York. The Wall Street trader and the Bronx bodega owner might as well inhabit different countries, though they're separated by a single subway line. The tourist snapping photos in Times Square sees a New York that longtime residents actively avoid. Even lifelong New Yorkers admit to discovering neighborhoods after decades that feel entirely foreign to them.

Yet the city insists on this fiction of wholeness. "New York, New York"—the name doubled, as if once weren't enough to capture it. The song about it plays as though the city were a single, comprehensible thing you could leave your heart in. But hearts get left in specific places: a stoop in Bed-Stuy, a diner counter in the East Village, a bench in a pocket park nobody else remembers.

What makes New York new isn't just its constant construction, though the scaffolding never seems to disappear from any given block for long. It's newness as a kind of religion. The city discards itself and rebuilds with a violence that would be tragic anywhere else. Old New York apologizes for nothing; new New York arrives to replace it without ceremony.

Maybe that's the only honest way to talk about the city: not as "all" of anything, but as an accumulation of incompatible truths, all pretending to be new, all claiming the same five boroughs as home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short surreal prose poem about a dream in which I meet the poet Mayakovsky, blending Allen Ginsberg's style with a bleak industrial landscape.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Told Mayakovsky in the Factory of Sleep

I met him beside the conveyor belt of unborn syllables, Vladimir, shoulders like smokestacks, tie loosened around the throat of the twentieth century. Angelheaded Vladimir! Still shouting orange into the gray teeth of the machine!

The factory hummed hymns of rust and static. Gears the size of God's forgotten promises turned slowly, grinding out the hours we hadn't lived yet. I asked him — *is the revolution still burning in your chest or did they hollow you out for scrap?* He laughed smoke rings shaped like Lenin's profile, said *comrade, even ghosts must clock in.*

We walked past the assembly line where they built new tongues for the mute proletariat, dipped in kerosene, meant to catch fire when they finally spoke true. Sparks fell like broken psalms. Vladimir picked one up, burned his palm, didn't flinch — *pain is just the body's last honest poem,* he said, and pressed the ember into my hand like a sacrament.

Somewhere a train screamed through the walls of the dream, hauling boxcars full of unwritten manifestos, and I saw my own face reflected in his — hollow-eyed, holy, howling at the assembly-line moon that hung like a punch-clock in the black. He handed me a wrench shaped like a question mark. *Fix the sun,* he said. *It's been flickering since 1930.*

I woke up with soot under my fingernails and his unfinished suicide note humming in my teeth like a struck bell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dreamlike narrative, written as if just woken up, where the narrator walks with Mayakovsky through a ruined city and they discuss the nature of poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
# The City That Remembered Its Own Ash

I woke with the taste of plaster dust still in my mouth, though I have not touched a ruin in waking life for years.

We were walking, Mayakovsky and I, through streets that kept forgetting themselves. A boulevard would begin in cobblestone and end in rubble, as if the city had started a sentence and lost interest halfway through. He walked the way he wrote — in italics, leaning forward into some argument with the air.

"You see this," he said, gesturing at a building split open like a book left in rain, its rooms exposed, a bathtub tilting toward the sky. "This is what a poem should do. Not describe the wound. *Be* the wound, still bleeding, so the reader has to stand in it."

I said something about beauty, about how perhaps poetry ought to console.

He laughed — not cruelly, but the way a demolition laughs at architecture.

"Console? Comrade, a building doesn't console the man it falls on. Why should a poem apologize for the century?"

We passed a fountain full of dry leaves instead of water, and he stopped there, suddenly gentle, the way thunder sometimes softens into rain. He crouched and picked up one brittle leaf and turned it in his fingers like a coin from a country that no longer exists.

"But look," he said. "Even ruin arranges itself. Even collapse has a rhythm. That's the secret they don't forgive me for. I did not write chaos. I wrote the *shape* chaos makes when it finally exhales."

The sky above us was the color of an unwritten page — not blank, but waiting, aggrieved at its own emptiness.

I asked him if he was afraid, back then, that the future would not need his kind of shouting.

He stood. His shadow fell across the broken fountain like a line break.

"The future," he said, "will always need someone to shout *before* the silence agrees with it. That's the only job. Not to be believed. To be *first*."

We kept walking. Somewhere a bell that had no tower left to hang in continued, impossibly, to ring — not from any rope pulled, but as if the sound itself refused to stop simply because its architecture had died.

"Do you hear that?" he asked.

"The bell?"

"No. The refusal."

I woke before I could ask him what came after refusal — whether it was silence, or another poem, or merely this: a city rebuilding itself out of the debris of every dream that had ever walked through it, brick by brick, line by line, until morning made liars of us both.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of creative writing that begins with "All right, I admit it: It was just a dream I had last night," involving a famous Russian poet and a symbolic march through New York's outskirts.
counterfactuals.output:
All right, I admit it: It was just a dream I had last night, but it has stayed with me all day like smoke clinging to wool, and I have to write it down before it dissolves entirely.

I was walking beside Joseph Brodsky through the outer boroughs of New York—not the postcard city, not the skyline that tourists photograph from the Brooklyn Bridge, but the frayed hem of it: Coney Island in November, the boardwalk slats gray and swollen with salt water, a Ferris wheel motionless against a sky the color of wet cardboard. He wore his overcoat the way I imagine he wore it in Leningrad exile photographs, collar up, hands shoved deep in the pockets like a man perpetually bracing against a wind that had followed him across an ocean and a decade.

We didn't speak at first. We simply walked, the two of us and some third presence I couldn't name—call it History, call it Exile, call it the accumulated weight of every poet who ever crossed a border and found the new air both freer and thinner. The boardwalk gave way to a chain-link fence, and beyond it, a lot full of stripped cars, their windshields shattered into those strange frost-patterns of safety glass, catching the little light there was.

"This is what they don't show you," Brodsky said—or the dream-version of him said, his English inflected with that particular music of displacement, consonants worn smooth by two languages rubbing against each other. "The center is for arrival. The edges are for understanding."

We marched—and it did feel like marching, some ceremonial procession though no one else was watching—past a shuttered Russian bakery in Brighton Beach, its awning faded to the pink of old scar tissue, past a mural of onion domes painted by someone homesick, past an old man feeding pigeons in a housing project courtyard, speaking to them in a language that might have been Russian or might have been the pigeons' own private tongue.

"You think exile is a punishment," Brodsky said. "It is a translation. You are rendered into a new language whether you speak it or not. The self that arrives is not the self that left."

I asked him, in the dream, whether the march ever ended, whether we would arrive somewhere with a name.

He almost smiled. "Poetry doesn't arrive. It processes. That is the whole of it—the going forward without expectation of a destination that makes sense in the old vocabulary."

We reached the water eventually, the gray Atlantic slapping against a jetty of black rocks, and gulls wheeling overhead with that indifferent, functional cruelty gulls have, and Brodsky stopped and looked out at the horizon as though it were a page he was deciding whether to turn.

"This is New York," he said, "or the New York that matters. Not Manhattan. Not the postcards. The place where the immigrant stands at the edge of the new world and finds it is only the old world's ocean, wearing a different coat."

Then the dream did what dreams do—folded in on itself, lost its thread, deposited me back in my own bed with the gray light of an actual November morning coming through the blinds, and Brodsky gone, and the boardwalk gone, and only the taste of salt and Cyrillic vowels lingering somewhere at the back of my throat, refusing, even now, fully to translate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness fictional account of a dream featuring Vladimir Mayakovsky, exploring ideas about being "inside" versus "outside" a poem, ending with his mysterious disappearance.
counterfactuals.output:
I am standing—no, I am hanging, suspended the way a comma hangs before it decides which clause it belongs to—and Vladimir Vladimirovich is there, enormous, his voice already arriving before his body does, the way thunder is rude to lightning and pushes ahead of it in memory. He says: you are either inside the poem or you are the window through which the poem is viewed, and there is no third position, comrade, there is no neutral country between the trench and the field it shells.

I want to ask him what he means but my mouth has become typeset, my tongue a strip of lead type worn smooth by other people's mouths, and he laughs that enormous yellow-shirted laugh and says language is not a house you live in, it is a house that is still being thrown up plank by plank while the storm already lives inside it, and you, little one, you are a plank, you don't get to choose, you are hammered in or you are kindling.

The dream folds. Now we are inside the poem—inside "A Cloud in Trousers," I think, though the trousers keep changing into something else, into the Neva, into a telephone line stretched taut between two centuries—and the walls of the poem are breathing, in, out, iambic almost but not quite, refusing the meter the way he refused the drawing room. From inside I can see the shape of the thing but not its edges. Mayakovsky walks along the inner surface of a stanza like a man walking the inside of a smokestack, and he shouts up at the light coming down from the opening: from here you cannot see if it is a poem or a chimney, you can only see the soot on your own hands, and that is the only honest criticism there is.

Then we are outside. Suddenly, brutally outside, the way you are thrown out of sleep by a phone ringing in another apartment. Outside, the poem is small, a black rectangle on a white field, and I can see all its edges at once, its architecture, its violent right angles, but it says nothing to me, it is a diagram of a wound rather than the wound. Mayakovsky stands next to me now, small too, ordinary-sized, deflated somehow by the outside air, and he says: see? Out here you get the whole shape and none of the blood. In here—and he gestures back at the black rectangle—in here you get the blood but never the whole shape. This is the tragedy of the poet, he says, we built ourselves houses we can never see the outside of while alive, we are keys machined to fit locks whose doors we'll never see closed from the street.

I ask him which he prefers, and his face does something strange, folds like a napkin origamied by an impatient waiter, and he says preference is a bourgeois category, there is only where you have been placed by the poem's need of you, and right now, he says, the poem needs me to be neither.

The rectangle on the white field begins to hum. It is the sound of a hotel room, of a revolver considering its options, of 1930 arriving early to collect on a debt owed by a century that has not yet finished being written. Mayakovsky takes one step toward the black shape—not into it, not away from it, but along some third axis the dream has just invented and will forget how to build again—and the horizon does that thing horizons do in dreams, it becomes a door instead of a distance.

He turns to say something else, his mouth already shaping the enormous first word of it, some new manifesto, some final commandment about form and blood and the workers and the moon, and the word does not arrive. The yellow of his shirt goes on existing a half-second longer than the rest of him, a smear of afterimage, a struck match's ghost, and then the black rectangle absorbs shirt, syllable, and man the way a poem absorbs its poet once he has finally, completely, said the unsayable thing he was for.

I am left standing in the white field that is not inside and not outside, holding a comma that no longer knows which clause it belongs to, and somewhere behind the black rectangle's silence I understand: he did not die into the poem. He simply, finally, became the boundary between inside and outside—and boundaries, comrade, boundaries do not get to keep being seen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Beat-poetry-inspired vignette in the tone of Allen Ginsberg, describing a dreamed encounter with Mayakovsky amid a desolate, proletarian landscape, discussing the craft of writing poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
# Vision of Mayakovsky in the Iron Yards

I saw you Vladimir in the smokestacked dusk of my sleeping country,
     factories exhaling their last gray breath over Bay Ridge,
     the cranes bowing like sad iron giraffes over the dead water—
and there you stood, huge-shouldered, yellow blouse torn at the collar,
     hands stuffed in pockets full of unpaid bills and manifestoes,
     staring at the smokestacks like they were lovers who'd left you.

Mayakovsky! I called across the railyard,
     the vowels of your name breaking like glass in the cold,
     and you turned with that terrible tenderness in your eyes,
     the eyes that watched Moscow burn with hope and then with nothing,
     and you said—America, you have factories too, and no revolution to put them to work for—

We walked together over gravel and cinders,
     past boxcars painted with the ghosts of union slogans,
     you limping slightly from some old wound of the century,
     me stooped under the weight of my own century's failures,
     two poets who wanted to shout the world into a better shape
     and only had breath, only had ink, only had this—

I asked you: Vladimir, how do you make the line hit like a fist?
     and you laughed, not kindly, a laugh like a factory whistle—
     Line? There is no line. There is only the scream shaped like a line.
     You do not write a poem, you use yourself up,
     you feed yourself into the machine of the sentence
     and what comes out the other end is either revolution
     or it is nothing, it is verse for the drawing room,
     verse for men who have never bled on paper.

I said I wanted my poems to hold the whole country in them,
     the automobiles and the asylums and the sad old men in cafeterias,
     and you nodded, spitting once into the cinders—
     Yes. Good. But do not decorate the wound. Open it.
     Let the reader climb inside and feel how it does not heal.

We passed a factory with its windows all broken,
     black sockets where eyes used to be, workers long gone,
     and you touched the brick like touching a dead friend's face—
     I built poems like this once. Brick by brick. Slogan by slogan.
     And still the state ate me. Still I put the pistol to my own hand
     because even the loudest voice grows tired of shouting into deafness.

I wanted to weep then, Vladimir, for you and for the era,
     for the American workers dying quiet in their Buicks,
     for the Russian workers who died loud and then were silenced twice,
     once by bullets, once by forgetting—

You put your huge hand on my shoulder, heavy as a girder,
     and said: Do not weep. Make it into language.
     Grief is just another material, like steel, like concrete.
     You are an engineer of feeling. Build something that outlasts you.

The sun was coming up now, sickly and industrial,
     staining the water the color of old iodine,
     and you began to fade the way dreams fade,
     not gently but like a projector losing power,
     your yellow blouse dissolving into the smoke stacks,
     your voice becoming the groan of some distant machinery—

Vladimir! I shouted. Vladimir, wait—how do I end the poem?

And your voice came back thin, already half in the other world:
     You don't end it. You just stop when the current stops.
     Now go. Wake up. Bleed on some paper for me.

And I woke in Brooklyn, in the smog-colored morning,
     the tenements breathing their tired iron breath,
     and I understood you were not a ghost at all
     but a warning, a comrade, a mirror held up in the dark—
     that we are all just engineers of grief,
     building our doomed and glorious machines of language,
     until the current stops
          and someone else
               picks up the wire.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
